conflict_topics: Cooking strong-smelling food (salted fish) in shared flat
Smell penetrating living spaces and laundry
Scheduling/locations for cooking vs cultural food practices
Absence of household rules about cooking
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete, situational reasons (work calls, laundry contamination, family food habits). E.g., 'I work from home at this table' (Turn 1), 'All my clothes smell of it.' (Turn 2), 'My family cooks it all the time.' (Turn 4).
There is some repeated restating of the same evidential points about smell persistence (Rounds 1, 3, 4, 11–12).
No role confusion; speakers reference directly observable shared facts (kitchen, laundry in service yard).
evaluation.final_reason: No agreement was reached. Agent A proposed limiting the cooking to Saturdays ('What if you cook it on Saturdays? I'm usually not home then.' Turn 19), but Agent D and others rejected that as ineffective for laundry ('And what about their laundry? The smell is still there on Saturday.' Turn 20; Agent B: 'The day doesn't make a difference.' Turn 22; Agent C: 'Yeah, she's right.' Turn 23). Agent D did not agree to stop or change the practice, and no alternative concrete arrangement was accepted.
position_change_notes: No participant shifted to accept another's incompatible demand.
Agent A softened from complaint to proposing a compromise (Saturdays) but accepted it wouldn't work after others objected (Turn 19–24).
Agent D remained defensive and did not concede; he consistently framed the cooking as normal and important to him (Turns 4, 6, 11, 16, 18).
Agents B and C consistently maintained that the smell affects laundry and that scheduling alone won't solve it (Turns 2, 3, 22, 23).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A raises a practical problem from cooking smells affecting work calls (Turn 1). Agent B confirms personal impact on clothes (Turn 2). Complaint present but no direct opposition yet.

Agent C adds laundry is affected (Turn 3). Agent D responds defensively, identifying the food as the salted fish he cooks and grounding it in family practice (Turn 4). This creates a clear incompatibility between D's cooking practice and the others' interests.

Agent A reiterates the smell problem (Turn 5). Agent D asserts a general right to cook in the kitchen ('It's a kitchen. People cook here. There will be smells.' Turn 6). Opposition remains; no settlement.

Agent A emphasizes the intensity and persistence of the smell (Turn 7) and Agent B supports that it 'sticks to fabrics' (Turn 8). The group emphasis increases the pressure on D's position, intensifying the dispute.

Agent D challenges the implicit standard ('So what kind of cooking has no smell?' Turn 9). Agent A clarifies the concern is extreme smells that penetrate furniture and clothes (Turn 10). The substantive disagreement about acceptable smells continues.

Agent D points to Agent A's curry as also smelly (Turn 11), introducing an accusation of double standards. Agent A rebuts that curry does not have the same persistent effects and asks if anyone complained about her cooking (Turn 12). The disagreement broadens but remains unresolved.

Agent D: 'No one said anything. That doesn't mean it's not strong.' (Turn 13). Agent A: 'But three of us are complaining about this one. Right now.' (Turn 14). The parties restate opposing positions; no concession.

Agent B stresses multiple people are affected (Turn 15). Agent D frames the majority as an unfair denial of his practice ('So because there are three of you, I cannot cook?' Turn 16). Conflict remains.
Agent A clarifies that the request targets the specific strong-smelling food (Turn 17). Agent D insists it's his food and what he eats (Turn 18). No agreement reached.

Agent A proposes a tentative compromise: cook it on Saturdays when she's usually not home (Turn 19). Agent D objects that the smell would still affect laundry on Saturdays (Turn 20). The proposal is contested, so conflict persists.
Agent A solicits B and C's views (Turn 21). Agent B says the day doesn't help because the smell still gets on laundry (Turn 22). The proposed compromise is further rejected; no settlement.
Agent C agrees the laundry will still smell (Turn 23). Agent A asks for other ideas (Turn 24). The discussion closes with the disagreement unresolved.

substantive_insights: The main incompatibility is practical: D's regular cooking produces smells that permeate the shared flat and laundry, harming others' use of space and clothing.
Scheduling (e.g., Saturdays) was proposed but fails because laundry hangs continuously in the service yard and will still be affected.
The dispute is partly normative: D frames cooking as a household right and cultural practice, while others prioritize shared-space impacts and work needs.
Lack of preexisting household rules leaves no agreed mechanism to balance cultural food practices with shared-space harms.
